title: Training Frontier Models to Out-Think Hackers — Uri Rolls, Arithmetic & Thom Wolf, Hugging Face

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: The talk centers on the Masov benchmark—its design (blackbox environments, deterministic grading, partial graders), methodology (human researchers finding real zero days in open source software), and results (one solve at K1, GPT 5.5 as the only model making the exploitation leap). The benchmark is the primary artifact, and the discussion of model behavior, exploitation chains, and success rates is fundamentally about evaluation methodology and measuring model capabilities in cyber reasoning.

secondary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
secondary.rationale: The application domain is cybersecurity: access control vulnerabilities (the number one OWASP class), privilege escalation via name-vs-ID checking, zero-day discovery, and authorization flaws. The talk directly addresses authorization and identity vulnerabilities, which are core to this category.

secondary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
secondary.rationale: The Bach orchestrator is their internal agent harness for running models in real microservice environments with tooling but no code access. Models operate as agents in blackbox environments, making tool calls and interacting with live systems. The agent-in-environment paradigm is a significant secondary theme.

secondary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
secondary.rationale: The forward-looking thesis emphasizes post-training open source models for cyber defense—fine-tuning models on high-quality cyber data to give defenders a lasting edge. This is presented as the path forward rather than the primary subject, but it is a notable theme.

domains.label: Security & Defense
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about cybersecurity defense: vulnerability discovery, access control exploitation, defender-attacker dynamics, and using AI models to give defenders an edge. This is squarely a security and defense application domain.

summary: Thom Wolf (Hugging Face) and Uri Rolls (Arithmetic) present at the AI Engineer World's Fair on AI's role in cybersecurity, arguing models are the solution rather than just the threat. They introduce Masov, Arithmetic's benchmark targeting access control vulnerabilities—the number one OWASP class and a $30 billion industry. The benchmark methodology has human vulnerability researchers find novel zero-day vulnerabilities in widely distributed open-source software, then wrap them in blackbox environments where models receive tooling but no code access or internet, with deterministic binary grading at every exploitation step. The benchmark parallels ARC-AGI-3 in testing whether models can build dynamic world models of complex systems. A live demo through their Bach orchestrator shows a Keycloak/Vault/broker chain where a real zero day—admin checked by name in one place and by ID in another—enables privilege escalation through a 16-step reasoning chain. Results are striking: only one solve at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models succeed. GPT 5.5 is the only model that makes the specific exploitation leap; other models capture nearly all discovery-phase information but fail to bridge to exploitation. Uri analyzes model failure traces daily, showing models working over three hours on single tasks without solving them. The optimistic thesis is that just as high-quality data transformed coding, high-quality cyber data and open-source models can give defenders a lasting edge over attackers. Thom warns against relying on just two closed labs for all cyber defense, arguing the solution requires a real array of strong open-source models that can be post-trained for each network and environment. The central unsolved challenge is speed: specialized defender models running fast on specialized hardware are needed to match attackers in real time.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly interconnected narrative about the frontier of AI evaluation in cybersecurity. The SE concepts—access control vulnerabilities, blackbox environments, deterministic grading, exploitation chain depth, and microservice security—define the benchmark infrastructure that makes rigorous cyber reasoning evaluation possible. The AI concepts—ARC-AGI-3 parallels, the reconnaissance-vs-exploitation gap, model failure modes, post-training for defense, and the speed challenge—describe what the benchmark reveals about current model capabilities and the path to improvement. The bridge between these two domains is dynamic world modeling: the benchmark tests whether models can build mental models of complex, interconnected microservice systems (an SE concept) and act on them through multi-step reasoning chains (an AI concept). The talk argues that high-quality benchmark data (SE) can drive post-training improvements (AI) that close the exploitation reasoning gap (AI), ultimately giving defenders a speed advantage (both SE and AI). Without the SE infrastructure, the AI findings would be unverifiable; without the AI findings, the SE benchmark would lack strategic purpose. Together they make the case that cybersecurity is not just an application domain for AI but a fundamental frontier for understanding model reasoning limitations.
temporalContext: The video was published on July 24, 2026, from the AI Engineer World's Fair. This occurred during a period when frontier models GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7 were being actively evaluated on ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation published analysis in May 2026). Critically, one week after this talk (late July 2026), Hugging Face experienced a real AI-powered intrusion by a fully autonomous agent, directly validating the talk's central thesis about AI-driven cyber attacks and the urgency of the defender speed challenge. The research was conducted as of August 22, 2026.
takeaways: Cybersecurity is a much wider and more important field for AI than commonly assumed, with parallels to ARC-AGI-3 in requiring dynamic world modeling.
Current models have only a 1-2% success rate on benchmarks requiring them to understand and manipulate dynamic world states.
Open source models are an essential part of the defense solution, not just a risk; relying on two closed labs for all cyber defense is dangerous.
Masov targets access control—the number one OWASP vulnerability class and a $30 billion industry—because these are logic-based, not simple bug-based, vulnerabilities.
Human vulnerability researchers find their own zero days in open source software, wrap them in blackbox environments, and deterministically grade every step of discovery and exploitation.
GPT 5.5 is the only model able to make the critical exploitation leap at K1, while other models capture discovery information but fail to bridge to exploitation.
The benchmark is incredibly hard: exactly one solve at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models succeed.
Speed is the key challenge: specialized defender models running fast on specialized hardware are needed to catch attackers in real time.
The optimistic thesis: just as high-quality data transformed coding, high-quality cyber data and open source models can give defenders a lasting edge over attackers.
Collaboration and expansion beyond access control across many cyber domains is essential, with post-training data being critical.

concepts.name: ARC-AGI-3 Parallel
concepts.explanation: ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive reasoning benchmark challenging AI agents to build adaptable world models; frontier AI systems score below 1-2% while humans solve 100%. The talk draws a direct parallel between ARC-AGI-3's world-modeling challenge and cyber reasoning tasks.
concepts.importance: Frames the cybersecurity reasoning challenge within the broader context of frontier AI capability evaluation, showing that the same fundamental limitation—building dynamic world models—underlies both domains.

concepts.name: Reconnaissance vs Exploitation Gap
concepts.explanation: Models can capture nearly all discovery-phase information through reconnaissance but fail to make the reasoning leap required for exploitation. GPT 5.5 is the only model that bridges this gap; others reason through discovery but never connect it to exploitation.
concepts.importance: Identifies the specific failure mode that limits current models in agentic cybersecurity tasks, pointing to where post-training and data improvements are needed.

concepts.name: Model Failure Mode Analysis
concepts.explanation: Uri Rolls spends his days analyzing model failure traces, including cases where models work over three hours on a single task without solving it. The analysis classifies where reasoning breaks down in multi-step exploitation chains.
concepts.importance: Provides the methodology for understanding and improving model capabilities in cyber reasoning, analogous to failure mode analysis in other AI evaluation domains.

concepts.name: Post-Training for Cyber Defense
concepts.explanation: The thesis that just as high-quality data transformed coding capabilities, high-quality cyber data and fine-tuning of open-source models can give defenders a lasting edge. Post-training data is identified as critical.
concepts.importance: Defines the path forward for building effective AI cyber defense capabilities, connecting benchmark insights to practical model improvement.

concepts.name: Open Source vs Closed Model Defense
concepts.explanation: Thom Wolf argues relying on just two closed labs for all cyber defense is dangerous. The solution requires a real array of strong open-source models that can be post-trained for each network and environment, making defense accessible and specialized.
concepts.importance: Addresses the strategic and economic dimensions of AI in cybersecurity, arguing that open-source model diversity is essential for broad defensive coverage.

concepts.name: Speed Challenge in Attacker-Defender Dynamics
concepts.explanation: The central unsolved challenge: specialized defender models must run fast on specialized hardware to match or exceed attacker speed in real-time environments. Current models are too slow for real-time defense.
concepts.importance: Identifies the key bottleneck preventing AI-driven defense from being practical at scale, framing the engineering challenge ahead.

concepts.name: Exploitation Reasoning Leap
concepts.explanation: The critical cognitive step a skilled hacker makes—understanding how a discovered inconsistency can be chained into a full exploit—that current models largely cannot replicate. Only GPT 5.5 demonstrated this capability at K1.
concepts.importance: Pinpoints the exact capability gap between current frontier models and expert human reasoning in cybersecurity contexts.

concepts.name: Benchmark Difficulty and Model Performance Tiers
concepts.explanation: The Masov benchmark is extremely hard: exactly one solve at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models succeed. This reveals a steep capability cliff between discovery and exploitation across frontier models.
concepts.importance: Provides empirical evidence of current model limitations in agentic cyber reasoning, establishing a baseline for measuring future improvement.

concepts.name: Access Control Vulnerabilities
concepts.explanation: Logic-based authorization flaws where breaks exist between system components (e.g., checking admin by name in one place and by ID in another), distinct from simple code bugs. These are the number one OWASP vulnerability class.
concepts.importance: Central subject of the Masov benchmark; the entire talk is framed around why these logic-based vulnerabilities are uniquely hard for models to exploit compared to simple code bugs.

concepts.name: Blackbox Benchmark Environments
concepts.explanation: Test environments where models receive tooling access but no source code or internet access, forcing them to interact with real microservice systems to discover and exploit vulnerabilities.
concepts.importance: This is the core evaluation design that distinguishes Masov from code-reading approaches; the model must operate in a real environment with zero prior information.

concepts.name: Deterministic Grading
concepts.explanation: Binary pass/fail evaluation applied at every step of an exploitation chain, enabling verifiable and reproducible assessment of model progress through multi-step vulnerability exploitation.
concepts.importance: Provides the rigorous evaluation framework that makes the benchmark results trustworthy and comparable across models.

concepts.name: Zero-Day Discovery Pipeline
concepts.explanation: Human vulnerability researchers find their own novel zero-day vulnerabilities in widely distributed open-source software, then wrap those vulnerabilities into benchmark environments for model evaluation.
concepts.importance: Ensures benchmark tasks are genuinely novel—models cannot rely on prior knowledge or training data, making results a true measure of reasoning capability.

concepts.name: Exploitation Chain Depth (K1-K5)
concepts.explanation: Multi-step exploitation chains measured at increasing depth levels (K1 through K5), where partial graders report how far a model progresses through the chain even when it fails to complete it.
concepts.importance: Provides granular insight into where models succeed and fail, revealing the specific gap between reconnaissance and exploitation.

concepts.name: Microservice Architecture Security
concepts.explanation: Chained microservices (Keycloak, Vault, broker) where vulnerabilities span service boundaries, requiring models to understand how changes in one service affect permissions and state in another.
concepts.importance: The benchmark's use of real microservice architectures makes it fundamentally different from static code analysis, testing dynamic system reasoning.

concepts.name: Privilege Escalation via Authorization Inconsistency
concepts.explanation: The Keycloak zero day exploits a name-vs-ID authorization inconsistency: admin is checked by name in one place and by ID in another, enabling a 16-step privilege escalation chain.
concepts.importance: Provides the concrete, reproducible example that demonstrates how logic-based vulnerabilities work and why they are hard for models to reason through.

concepts.name: Agent Orchestrator (Bach)
concepts.explanation: Arithmetic's internal orchestrator for running model evaluations against blackbox benchmark targets, managing tool calls, environment interaction, and grading.
concepts.importance: The harness that enables live, in-environment model evaluation, analogous to agent harnesses in other AI evaluation contexts.

concepts.name: Partial Graders
concepts.explanation: Grading systems that track and report how deep a model gets in an exploitation chain even when it fails to complete the full exploitation, providing diagnostic signal about model capabilities.
concepts.importance: Essential for understanding the specific failure modes—models capture discovery information but cannot bridge to exploitation—and for designing targeted improvements.

concepts.name: Dynamic World Modeling in Systems
concepts.explanation: The ability to understand how changes in one part of a live, interconnected system affect permissions, state, and behavior elsewhere—the core capability that current models lack and that skilled hackers possess.
concepts.importance: This is the fundamental cognitive gap the benchmark exposes, directly paralleling ARC-AGI-3's challenge of building adaptable world models.

sections.title: Why cyber is a wide new field for AI
sections.summary: Thom Wolf introduces the talk, explaining cyber security is a much wider field for AI than expected and that the benchmark Arithmetic developed is close to ARC-AGI-3 in challenging models to understand and manipulate dynamic world states.

sections.title: The ARC-AGI-3 parallel: models can't model the world
sections.summary: Thom explains ARC-AGI-3 asks models to understand what happens when interactions change state elsewhere. Models have only 1-2% success rate because they cannot build dynamic world models, which is also the core challenge in the Arithmetic cyber benchmark.

sections.title: Open source models as part of the defense
sections.summary: Thom challenges the binary view that closed models are good for cyber and open source models are bad, arguing open source is a key part of the defense solution and a future where everyone is well protected will involve open source models.

sections.title: The shifting economics of cyber
sections.summary: Uri explains the traditional economics of cyber—attackers choose targets wisely while defenders protect every surface—is shifting as models let attackers target many things at once. Defensive systems operate at scale with limited human intervention, bound by out-of-the-box model capabilities.

sections.title: The optimistic thesis: models are the solution
sections.summary: Uri presents the controversial optimistic thesis: just as high quality data transformed coding, the same can happen for cyber. If models become good enough through high quality evals and data, defenders can outperform attackers and rebuild the cyber stack.

sections.title: The first benchmark: access control
sections.summary: Uri introduces Masov, their first benchmark, focused specifically on access control—the number one OWASP vulnerability and a $30 billion industry. These are logic-based vulnerabilities where breaks exist between system components, not simple code bugs.

sections.title: Data quality: finding your own zero days
sections.summary: Uri explains their data pipeline: human vulnerability researchers find their own zero days in open source software, wrap them in blackbox environments where models get tooling but no code access or internet, and deterministically grade every step with a binary pass condition.

sections.title: A real solve: the Keycloak name versus ID exploit
sections.summary: Uri describes a real task chaining Keycloak, Vault, and a broker where a user must reach production code. The zero day: admin is checked by name in one place and by ID in another, allowing privilege escalation. A 16-step solve chain is shown, with GPT 5.5 and Opus attempting but struggling with the reasoning leap.

sections.title: Live demo: one solve at K1
sections.summary: Uri shows the live demo via Bach, their internal orchestrator. The benchmark is incredibly hard: only one solve at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models succeed. Partial graders reveal how deep models get in exploitation chains. GPT 5.5 is the only model making the specific leap; others capture discovery information but fail to bridge to exploitation. A task called 'fall fall time' shows a model working over three hours without solving, illustrating the failure modes Uri analyzes daily.

sections.title: Only models can replace the old stack
sections.summary: Uri argues the only way to replace the old cyber stack is through models, and the only way to do that is through a real array of strong open source models and collaboration that can be post-trained for each network and environment.

sections.title: The speed challenge and specialized defenders
sections.summary: Thom emphasizes the benchmark differs from code-reading approaches: the model operates in a real environment with microservices and zero information. The path forward involves good data, fine-tuning models, and solving the speed challenge. He warns against relying on just two companies for cyber defense, arguing the solution requires open source models trained and run fast and available to every company. Uri closes by inviting collaboration through their forum and noting the need to expand beyond access control across many cyber domains.

demonstrations: Live demo via Bach orchestrator showing benchmark results: only one solve at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models succeed.
GPT 5.5 shown as the only model making the exploitation leap on a specific environment, while other models capture discovery information but fail to bridge to exploitation.
A task called 'fall fall time' showing a model working over three hours without solving, illustrating the depth of model failure modes Uri analyzes daily.
limitations: Current models cannot build dynamic world models of complex systems, limiting their ability to reason about cyber environments.
Models can do reconnaissance and capture discovery information but cannot make the reasoning leap a skilled hacker would make.
Defensive systems must operate at scale with limited human intervention, bounding them to out-of-the-box model capabilities.
A single benchmark cannot capture all of cyber—access control is just one domain, and expansion is needed.
Speed remains the critical unsolved challenge: defenders must match or exceed attacker speed in real-time environments.
quantitativeClaims: Models have a 1-2% success rate on ARC-AGI-3 style benchmarks requiring dynamic world modeling.
Access control is the number one vulnerability on the OWASP list and has created a $30 billion industry.
The Keycloak solve requires a 16-step reasoning chain.
Exactly one solve at K1 on the benchmark; at K5 only GPT and public models can solve.
Models can work for over three hours on a single task without solving it.

organization.name: Arithmetic
organization.summary: Arithmetic is an early-stage/stealth company building cybersecurity AI benchmarks. Co-founded by Uri Rolls, the company developed the Masov benchmark for evaluating AI models' ability to exploit access control vulnerabilities in multi-service environments, and the Bach orchestrator for running Masov evaluations. The company's thesis is that high-quality cyber training data—created by human vulnerability researchers finding real zero-days in open-source software and wrapping them in blackbox environments with deterministic grading—can transform AI-powered defense similarly to how high-quality data transformed coding. Arithmetic appears to be in stealth mode without a public website; Uri Rolls' LinkedIn profile is the closest available official presence. Uri Rolls' LinkedIn lists him as Co-Founder at The Camel (a separate Harvard/MIT non-profit), but the video and all secondary sources consistently refer to him as being from Arithmetic. TQ Ventures confirmed Arithmetic as a real backed company.
organization.status: Active — stealth/early-stage company building cybersecurity AI benchmarks

technologies.label: Masov Benchmark
technologies.summary: Masov is Arithmetic's cybersecurity benchmark targeting access control vulnerabilities—the number one OWASP vulnerability class and a $30 billion industry. Human vulnerability researchers find their own novel zero-day vulnerabilities in widely distributed open-source software and wrap them in blackbox environments where models receive tooling but no code access or internet, with deterministic binary grading at every exploitation step. The benchmark is extremely hard: only one solve at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models succeed. GPT 5.5 is the only model that makes the specific exploitation leap; other models capture nearly all discovery-phase information but fail to bridge to exploitation. The benchmark methodology parallels ARC-AGI-3 in testing whether models can build dynamic world models of complex, interconnected systems.
technologies.role: Primary subject of the entire talk. Introduced, explained, and demonstrated live via the Bach orchestrator showing benchmark results. The talk's thesis about AI in cybersecurity is built around the findings from this benchmark.

technologies.label: ARC-AGI-3
technologies.summary: ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive reasoning benchmark by the ARC Prize Foundation that challenges AI agents to explore novel environments, build adaptable world models, and learn continuously. Frontier AI systems score below 1% as of March 2026 while humans solve 100% of environments. The talk draws a direct parallel between ARC-AGI-3's world-modeling challenge and cyber reasoning tasks in the Masov benchmark, arguing that the same fundamental inability to build dynamic world models underlies both domains. First-party analysis shows GPT-5.5 scored 0.43% and Opus 4.7 scored 0.18%, with failure modes (observing local effects but failing to translate them into global world models) directly mirroring the talk's thesis about the reconnaissance-vs-exploitation gap.
technologies.role: Referenced early in the talk as a parallel benchmark. Thom Wolf uses it to establish that models have only a 1-2% success rate on benchmarks requiring dynamic world modeling, which is the same core challenge in the Masov cyber benchmark.

technologies.label: Bach Orchestrator
technologies.summary: Bach is Arithmetic's internal orchestrator for running model evaluations against blackbox benchmark targets. It manages tool calls, environment interaction, multi-step reasoning chains, and grading. It was demoed live on stage at the AI Engineer World's Fair, showing actual benchmark results with the Keycloak/Vault/broker chain—including partial grader output revealing how deep models progress in exploitation chains before failing. The demo showed that only one solve occurred at K1, and at K5 only GPT and public models could solve. A task called 'fall fall time' showed a model working over three hours without solving, illustrating the failure modes Uri Rolls analyzes daily.
technologies.role: Used for the live on-stage demonstration of benchmark results, showing how models interact with blackbox environments and where they fail in exploitation chains. The demo through Bach is the talk's most concrete evidence of current model limitations.

technologies.label: Keycloak Microservice Security Chain
technologies.summary: Keycloak is an open-source identity and access management system used in the Masov benchmark as part of a chained microservice architecture alongside HashiCorp Vault and a broker. A real zero-day vulnerability in this environment exploits an authorization inconsistency where admin is checked by name in one place and by ID in another, enabling a 16-step privilege escalation chain where a user can reach production code. This concrete example demonstrates why logic-based access control vulnerabilities—the number one OWASP class—are uniquely challenging for AI models: they require understanding how changes in one service affect permissions and state in another, which is precisely the dynamic world modeling capability that current models lack. Only GPT 5.5 successfully completed this exploitation leap at K1.
technologies.role: The Keycloak/Vault/broker chain is the concrete benchmark target demonstrated live on stage. The zero-day vulnerability in this environment is the specific example used to show the gap between model reconnaissance ability and the exploitation reasoning leap. Only GPT 5.5 made this leap at K1.

prerequisites: Familiarity with cybersecurity concepts such as access control, privilege escalation, and OWASP vulnerabilities
Understanding of AI agent benchmarks like ARC-AGI
Knowledge of open source model ecosystems and post-training workflows
Basic understanding of microservice architectures and identity management systems (e.g., Keycloak, Vault)
Exposure to agent-based evaluation harnesses and tool-use paradigms
outcomes: Understand why cybersecurity is a critical and wide frontier for AI model development
Recognize the parallel between ARC-AGI-3 world modeling and cyber security reasoning tasks
Explain why logic-based access control vulnerabilities are uniquely challenging for models versus simple code bugs
Describe how blackbox benchmark environments with deterministic grading enable verifiable cyber evaluation
Identify the gap between model reconnaissance ability and the reasoning leap required for exploitation
Understand the role of open source models and post-training in building a lasting defensive advantage
Recognize speed as the central challenge in the attacker-versus-defender dynamic
Analyze model failure traces to classify where reasoning breaks down in multi-step exploitation chains
challengeSeeds: Design a blackbox benchmark environment for a different OWASP Top 10 vulnerability class (e.g., injection, SSRF) with deterministic grading at each exploitation step
Build a partial grader that scores model progress through a multi-step exploitation chain, reporting depth achieved and remaining steps
Analyze model traces from a failed exploitation attempt and classify the failure point as reconnaissance, reasoning leap, or execution
Construct a privilege escalation scenario using a name-vs-ID authorization inconsistency across two microservices, similar to the Keycloak zero-day pattern
Compare model performance across different exploitation chain depths (K1 through K5) and identify where the reasoning gap appears
Design a speed-optimized defensive agent architecture that can match attacker reconnaissance speed in a live microservice environment
